Changes are displayed only if they are statistically significant (P < 0.05 in a two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test) and set to zero otherwise.DiscussionGenFocal leverages generative AI to overcome the limitations of traditional climate downscaling methods. It is trained directly on coarse climate simulations and weather reanalysis data, eliminating the need for costly regional climate model simulations to establish temporally aligned training data22 while explicitly accounting for coarse model biases. By leveraging historical reanalysis to correct these systematic biases, GenFocal provides a means to observationally constrain future climate projections, analogous to recent transfer learning frameworks that blend historical observations with multi-model ensembles to reduce projection uncertainty31. Moreover, it is designed to capture the spatiotemporal, multivariate statistics of climate data accurately, addressing key limitations of statistical downscaling methods, such as BCSD and STAR-ESDM, which are incapable of modelling the complex interdependency of multiple variables. This enables GenFocal to quantify the uncertainty of TCs and other compound extreme events robustly and efficiently. Such tasks have traditionally required narrowly focused, bespoke statistical emulators or computationally expensive dynamical downscaling.The practical implications of our method are significant for downstream applications that demand physically consistent localized climate data. For instance, accurate spatial correlation modelling can improve system-wide energy grid planning by estimating the risk of concurrent heat extremes that increase energy demand and vulnerability of power lines3,32. In addition, the ability to capture inter-variable correlations, such as those between temperature and humidity, is essential for predicting the heat index, which has direct applications in public health, food production33, energy demand forecasting32,34 and disaster preparedness35. Furthermore, directly modelling temporal correlations improves risk estimates for extended extreme events, such as prolonged heatwaves and TCs, offering more reliable insights for resilience policies36,37. By providing a full probabilistic characterization of climate effects, GenFocal enables assessing risks associated with compound hazards involving any number of meteorological extremes interacting across space and time.Finally, GenFocal opens the way for downscaling efficiently large ensembles of climate projections, a computationally intractable task for physics-based downscaling approaches. This is a crucial capability for present and future risk assessments of regional extremes and rare events, such as TCs, particularly as advances in AI-accelerated climate simulation38,39,40 combined with advances in climate modelling and larger ensembles41 continue expanding our ability to sample global climate uncertainty.MethodsGenerative models used by GenFocalGenFocal is a two-step framework: first, a temporal sequence of consecutive climate states, \(y\in {\mathcal{Y}}\), which is coarse in scale and biased, is debiased into an intermediate sequence on the manifold \({\mathcal{Y}}{\prime}\) that is consistent with a sequence of coarse-grained weather states \(C{\prime} x\) where \(x\in {\mathcal{X}}\), the high-resolution weather manifold. A subsequent super-resolution step increases the spatiotemporal resolution of the debiased sequence while preserving temporal coherence. This two-stage design decouples learning the debiasing and the super-resolution operations, enabling ‘drop-in’ replacement of alternative debiasing operations, as explored in Supplementary Information, section 9.6.Super-resolutionWe construct \(C{\prime}\) as a coarsening operation by downsampling the ERA5 data from 2-hourly and 0.25° to daily and 1.5°, thus forming pairs of aligned data samples \((y{\prime} =C{\prime} {x}_{i},{x}_{i})\). To learn the super-resolution operation, that is, the inverse of the downsampling, we use a conditional diffusion model42,43, popularized by latest advances in image and video generation. We take advantage of the previous knowledge that a spatially interpolated linear mapping \({\mathcal{I}}(y{\prime} )\) already contains a strong approximation of the mean statistics of x by modelling the residual \(r:= x-{\mathcal{I}}(y{\prime} )\). As such we use the conditional diffusion model to sample from \(p(r| y{\prime} )\) and then add the sampled residual back to \({\mathcal{I}}(y{\prime} )\) to obtain the final output of the super-resolution.The conditional diffusion model learns a neural network based denoiser to iteratively refine a noisy version of the residual r + εσ to its clean version r. The noise is controlled by a scaled Gaussian variable \(\varepsilon \sim {\mathcal{N}}(0,1)\) where the scale σ is sampled from a refinement scheduling distribution \({\mathcal{Q}}\). The denoiser Dθ is thus trained to minimize the loss function between the refined and the clean residuals:$$\ell (\theta )={{\mathbb{E}}}_{x\in {\mu }_{x}}{{\mathbb{E}}}_{\sigma \sim {\mathcal{Q}}(\sigma )}{{\mathbb{E}}}_{\varepsilon \sim {\mathcal{N}}(0,1)}\parallel {D}_{\theta }(r+\epsilon \sigma ,\sigma ,y{\prime} )-r{\parallel }^{2}.$$
                    (1)
                Once learned, the denoiser Dθ is used to construct a stochastic differential equation-based sampler that refines a Gaussian noise signal into a clean residual:$${\mathrm{d}}{r}_{\tau }=-2{\dot{\sigma }}_{\tau }{\sigma }_{\tau }{D}_{\theta }\left({r}_{\tau },{\sigma }_{\tau },y{\prime} \right)\,{\mathrm{d}}\tau +\sqrt{2{\dot{\sigma }}_{\tau }{\sigma }_{\tau }}\,{\mathrm{d}}{\omega }_{\tau },$$
                    (2)
                in diffusion time τ from τ = τmax to 0, and initial condition \({r}_{{\tau }_{{\rm{max}}}} \sim {\mathcal{N}}(0,{\sigma }_{{\tau }_{{\rm{max}}}}^{2}I)\), where \({\sigma }_{\tau }:{\mathbb{R}}\to {\mathbb{R}}\) is the diffusion-time-dependent noise schedule, controlled by \({\mathcal{Q}}(\sigma )\). A more comprehensive description of the diffusion model is included in Supplementary Information, section 9.5.1, along with implementation details.While the model Dθ is trained on short sequences such as one to a few days, we use an inference procedure to sample extended temporal sequences (spanning multiple months, for example). The procedure achieves temporal coherence through domain decomposition, where each shorter temporal period is a domain and overlapping domains are guided to coherence and contiguity. Details are provided in Supplementary Information, section 9.5.3.DebiasingDue to the lack of alignment between data sampled from \({\mathcal{Y}}\) and \({\mathcal{Y}}{\prime}\), we seek a map between their sample distributions. This is a weaker notion than the sample-to-sample correspondence offered by physics-based downscaling methods. However, as demonstrated in this work, achieving a statistical distribution match can effectively debias while remaining computationally advantageous and generating plausible sampled states.We leverage the idea of rectified flows44 by constructing the debiasing map T as the solution map of an ordinary differential equation given by$${\frac{{\mathrm{d}}y}{{\mathrm{d}}\tau }}={\bf{v}}_{\phi }(y,\tau )\qquad \,\text{for}\,\tau \in [0,1],$$
                    (3)
                whose vector field vϕ(x, τ) is parametrized by a neural network (see Supplementary Information, section 9.4.3 for further details). By identifying the input of the map as the initial condition y0 = y(τ = 0), we have the solution as the mapping T(y) ≔ y(τ = 1). We train vϕ by minimizing loss$$\ell (\phi )={{\mathbb{E}}}_{\tau \sim {\mathcal{U}}[0,1]}{{\mathbb{E}}}_{({y}_{0},{y}_{1}) \sim \pi \in \Pi ({\mu }_{y},{\mu }_{y{\prime} })}\parallel ({y}_{1}-{y}_{0})-{\bf{v}}_{\phi }({y}_{\tau },\tau ){\parallel }^{2},$$
                    (4)
                where yτ = τy1 + (1 − τ)y0. \(\Pi ({\mu }_{y},{\mu }_{y{\prime} })\) is the set of couplings observing the marginal distributions of \({\mathcal{Y}}\) and \({\mathcal{Y}}{\prime}\) respectively. Once vϕ is learned, we debias any given y by solving (3) from τ = 0 to τ = 1 using the fourth-order Runge–Kutta ordinary differential equation solver.Analogous to super-resolution, we also learn a debiasing map that takes into consideration a temporal sequence of climate variables. In Supplementary Information, section 9.4, we describe a simple way to achieve this as well as other important implementation details, such as selection of the coupling \(\Pi ({\mu }_{y},{\mu }_{y{\prime} })\) (see Supplementary Information, section 10.6 for an ablation study of different choices) and parametrization of vϕ with various neural architecture choices.Evaluation protocols and metricsThe downscaling methods are evaluated in two categories of metrics. The first set of metrics evaluates the discrepancy between the distributions of the downscaled climate data and the corresponding ERA5 weather data. Three types of discrepancy are measured. The first measures the univariate differences at each site, which are averaged in space to give rise to mean absolute bias, Wasserstein distance and percentile mean absolute error. The second measures spatial correlation and temporal spectrum errors. The last type measures correlation discrepancies among different variables such as tail dependence, an important quantity for compound extremes. Supplementary Information, section 7 provides detailed definitions of the evaluation metrics.The second category of metrics is application-specific. In this work, we focus on North Atlantic TCs and severe and prolonged heat events over CONUS. In either case, non-trivial processing is performed on the output variables to compute composite variables (such as heat indices, the number of heat streak days) and TC occurrences and tracks. Evaluation metrics vary and we describe them in detail in Supplementary Information, section 8.

items.title: Space sustainability beyond ‘zero debris’: from orbital safety to circular materials
items.body:

Space sustainability beyond ‘zero debris’: from orbital safety to circular materials
                        Axel Solt-Rindler 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-6151-84901,2, Elisabeth Billich1,2, Johanna Sperl3, Werner Engel3, Bernhard Seifert3 & …Christian Hansmann1,2 Show authors

Communications Engineering
                            volume 5,  Article number: 166 (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
                                
    
        
            
            
                
            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

Space sustainability rests on the peaceful and socioeconomic use of space. Current measures focus on maintaining orbital trafficability, largely following a linear material flow, neglecting impacts on Earth’s atmosphere and environment. A holistic approach should extend concern from orbital safety and ground casualty risk to full circularity of spacecraft materials.

Subjects
                
                    
                        
                            Aerospace engineering
                        
                        
                            Composites
                        
                        
                            Environmental health

Current practiceThe declaration adopted at the Vienna UNISPACE III Conference in 1999, which mandated the development of a “blueprint for the peaceful uses of outer space in the twenty‑first century”, is widely regarded as an early political foundation for the sustainable use of space1. It anticipated later governance efforts such as the “Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines” adopted by COPUOS in 20072. Over the subsequent decades, space sustainability has become a central concern amid the rapid expansion and commercialization of orbital activities, with a strong emphasis on preserving a safe and predictable orbital environment. Current frameworks, including international guidelines and agency‑level initiatives, concentrate primarily on maintaining orbital safety through debris mitigation, collision avoidance, passivation and post‑mission disposal, typically operationalized via orbital lifetime limits and quantified casualty‑risk constraints3.Within this regime, “design for demise” (D4D) has become a key engineering principle: satellites and upper stages are increasingly designed, so that their components disintegrate and burn up during atmospheric re‑entry, minimizing the probability that surviving fragments reach the ground and keeping casualty risk below 1 × 10−4 3 This practice has redistributed the risk burden between the orbit and the Earth’s surface, but it largely omits explicit consideration of upper‑atmospheric consequences arising from the demise process itself. In effect, current standards treat the atmosphere as an unproblematic terminal sink, rather than as a sensitive component of the coupled Earth–space environmental system.Emerging considerationsEmerging analyses indicate that satellite re‑entry is unlikely to be environmentally neutral, particularly as launch rates and number of objects in orbit, most of which small satellites, increased over 250 % between 2020 and 20254. During high‑enthalpy re‑entry, spacecraft materials undergo ablation, fragmentation and oxidation, producing metal and nitrogen oxides and carbonaceous particles that are injected into the middle and upper atmosphere5. For typical low‑Earth‑orbit (LEO) satellites, aluminium‑rich structures can generate on the order of tens of kilograms of alumina (Al₂O₃) nanoparticles per satellite. These particles may persist in the upper atmosphere for years to decades, with estimated sedimentation times of up to approximately 30 years to reach stratospheric ozone layers, yet their potential impacts on radiative balance, heterogeneous chemistry and ozone remain poorly constrained by observations and models6.As constellations scale to tens of thousands of units and re‑entries become a routine element of the space economy, cumulative emissions from conventional, metal‑dominated structures may become non‑negligible in comparison with natural and other anthropogenic sources7. This raises a central question for materials science and space governance alike: can the routine incineration of satellites into the upper atmosphere remain the default endpoint of a sustainable space system, or must material choices and architectures be re‑examined with atmospheric effects in mind?Demisable, low‑impact materialsMaterial standards and related ECSS requirements, such as ECSS-U-AS-10C Rev.2 (adoption of ISO 24113:2023), address space-debris mitigation, re-entry casualty risk and design-for-demise considerations, while dedicated ECSS material standards govern thermal-vacuum outgassing (ECSS-Q-ST-70-02C), resistance to particle and UV radiation (ECSS-Q-ST-70-06C), and resistance to atomic oxygen for materials exposed on external surfaces in LEO (ECSS-Q-ST-70C Rev.2). Within this context, aluminium alloys combine high specific strength with good environmental stability in space and are therefore widely used for primary and secondary structures. However, re‑entry‑derived metal‑oxide emissions and the energy and resource‑intensive production of aluminium motivate the exploration of alternative approaches that reduce environmental impacts across the life cycle.A promising response is to tailor spacecraft for demisability and low environmental impact at the end of life. Strategies include the use of low‑melting or fragmenting alloys in non‑critical elements, polymeric or composite structures designed to ablate completely and foamed or hollow configurations that promote breakup and oxidation8. Such choices can be applied selectively to secondary structures, bracketry, instrument housings or sacrificial elements, complementing more conservative materials in propulsion, pressure vessels and other critical subsystems. Within this broader landscape of demisable, low‑impact solutions, bio-based materials such as wood offer a distinctive combination of renewable resource base, with relatively low carbon footprint in production and intrinsically benign re‑entry behaviour, making them a particularly attractive option for sustainable, demisable spacecraft components. Beyond wood, other circular material classes merit parallel consideration, including natural-fibre-reinforced composites, thermosets and thermoplastics derived from renewable or waste feedstocks, including biodegradable polymers such as polylactic acid (PLA). High-performance thermoplastics such as PEEK may further support design-for-demise and have already been shown to improve the demisability of critical fasteners relative to steel or titanium baselines9.Quantitatively grounding the choice among these candidates requires a full life-cycle perspective. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), following the ISO 14040/44 framework and adapted by ESA for space systems, provides an established method for quantifying environmental impacts across the mission life cycle. Recent work further extends conventional LCA by combining the Environmental Footprint 3.1 method with a dedicated Space Debris Indicator, allowing end-of-life scenarios, including natural re-entry, controlled re-entry and graveyard disposal, to be compared across terrestrial, atmospheric and orbital impact domains10.Wood as An Illustrative CaseWood is a renewable material that can exhibit high specific strength and stiffness and has been used for centuries in load‑bearing applications. Recent demonstrations, such as the LignoSat concept11, indicate that suitably selected and processed solid wood can, in principle, satisfy key functional requirements for small satellites, including acceptably low outgassing and stable behaviour under radiation and thermal cycling. In LEO, typical terrestrial challenges of moisture protection and fire safety are largely absent, while combustibility and a very low inorganic content (app. 1 %, ref. 12) make wood well aligned with D4D: during atmospheric re‑entry, its near‑complete oxidation and low ash yield significantly limit the release of inorganic nanoparticles compared with metallic structures. Recent plasma-wind-tunnel experiments under representative LEO re-entry conditions support the high demisability of wood-based structures, with a beech–balsa panel completely demising in less than 30 s at temperatures of up to 2000 K and predominantly CN, CH, C₂, Na, and K, but no metal oxides, being detected among the ablation species13. Nevertheless, systematic qualification under space‑relevant conditions remains an important area for future research rather than a solved problem. Key open questions include long‑term performance under thermal cycling in vacuum, creep and relaxation in complex load paths, response to space radiation and atomic oxygen at LEO altitudes and the design of robust joining technologies and interfaces with metals, composites and electronics especially for launch conditions. Wood products should therefore be investigated not as a universal replacement for established aerospace alloys, but as a strategically useful option for well‑chosen subsystems in which its demisability and resource advantages can be realized without compromising safety or reliability. Potential near-term applications include secondary structural panels, brackets and housings. In a recent 5 kg 3U CubeSat case study, the aluminium structure accounted for 60 % of total satellite mass, illustrating that even partial substitution of suitable structural components could address a meaningful fraction of the demisable mass10.Adapting the Space Sustainability ParadigmMaterials demising in an environmentally less harmful manner, represent an important advance, but they still operate largely within a fundamentally linear “launch–operate–burn‑up” logic. Even when the material itself is renewable or has a benign re‑entry signature, using it once and discarding it into the atmosphere falls short of a truly sustainable paradigm for a mature space economy. Another step is to view spacecraft mass not only as something that must ultimately vanish cleanly, but as a resource that should be preserved, maintained and, where possible, recirculated within the space environment.From this perspective, concepts funded by the European Space Agency (ESA), the European Defence Fund (EDF) and within the HORIZON Europe program increasingly target such as in-orbit satellite refuelling as a key enabler for extending spacecraft operational lifetimes while aligning with the objectives of the ESA Zero-Debris Charter. In‑orbit servicing, repair and refurbishment, life‑extension missions and the recovery and reuse of major elements such as launch stages all point toward treating spacecraft and their materials as assets rather than consumables. To unlock these possibilities at scale, materials, interfaces and structures must be designed not only for demisability and low atmospheric impact, but also for inspectability, repairability and eventual reprocessing under space conditions, including standardized interfaces and modular architectures that facilitate component removal and reuse. Such a shift would align space sustainability more closely with circular‑economy thinking, extending concern from how satellites end their service life to how long, and how wisely, their materials are used. This will ultimately require regulatory and economic frameworks that reward extended lifetimes, reuse and low‑impact demise alongside compliance with debris‑mitigation and casualty‑risk guidelines14.

items.title: An historic fishery collapse driven by socioeconomic and environmental factors
items.body:

Article

An historic fishery collapse driven by socioeconomic and environmental factors
                        Rudi Voss 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4299-87911,2, Jörn O. Schmidt 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4420-65322, Oliver Lehmann2, Daniel Okamoto3, Patrick Polte4, Kira Lancker5, Anja Grunwald6 & …Marco Scotti7,8 Show authors

Nature Sustainability
                             (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
                                
    
        
            
            
                
            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

AbstractIn the Late Middle Ages, the western Baltic herring fishery played a central role in Europe. Salted herring was the basis for welfare and political power. We make use of a 450-year time series of Baltic herring catches (1200–1650), to identify which factors drove the herring catch dynamics during different phases of our time series. By the year 1570, the fishery suddenly collapsed, causing large-scale dislocations in trade, with major social and political consequences. Using a recently established bioeconomic stock assessment method based on catch and price data, in tandem with a loop analysis, we find that a combination of climate change, overfishing and socioeconomic factors can explain the drastic collapse of the fishery. The results underline the need for interdisciplinary approaches, including social sciences, to understand the dynamics of fishery systems. This has relevance for fisheries management today, in the Baltic and elsewhere.

Explore related subjects
            Discover the latest articles and news in related subjects.
            
                
                    
                        
                            Ecological modelling
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Environmental economics
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Governance
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Marine biology
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Sustainability
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Historical Ecology of Marine Fisheries and Ecosystems

MainFor nearly 300 years (1280–1570), the western Baltic herring fishery, located in a small sound area between Denmark and Sweden (Sound fishery; Supplementary Fig. 1) was the main producer of salted herring in Europe1. From the British Isles to Middle and Eastern Europe and all the way to Northern Italy, western Baltic herring was traded. During the autumn fishing season (15 August to 9 October), fairs held near small towns became important centres of commerce. A time series of herring catches in the western Baltic Sea has been reconstructed by ref. 1 from fragmentary historical evidence by combining direct records with indirect economic and environmental indicators. Where available, the authors relied on concrete data from customs records, toll books, royal pre-emption (kongekøb) accounts and other archival sources that reported trade volumes for specific years and locations (see Supplementary Information for a detailed description of the creation of the time series in English language; the original publication is in German). According to the authors, the Sound fishery can roughly be described by four phases, which show some peculiar similarities to the progression of events that led to collapses in modern fisheries (for example, the Atlantic northwest cod fishery): (1) expansion, (2) stagnation, (3) boom phase and (4) collapse (Fig. 1). Over the analysed time horizon, the fishery had no meaningful harvest or entry restrictions, although limited gear restrictions and lump-sum taxation did exist in certain areas2.Fig. 1: Estimated catches of western Baltic autumn-spawning herring as well as temperature anomalies in the period 1200–1650.Full size imageSmoothed profile of catches taken in the Sound fishery are shown as a dark blue area; catches in the whole western Baltic are indicated by the striped blue area. Yellow and light-blue lines in the period 1500–1600 show decadal means and yearly catch values, respectively. Specific historic events are indicated. The following URLs provide short YouTube videos of ‘contemporary witnesses’: The viking, https://youtu.be/5xI24Oam-eM?si=wZeI57etvytzp5YY; The fisher, https://youtu.be/ykzvIjtLmCw?si=M3d7IFi4PYD1_56W; The toll-keeper, https://youtu.be/FBeg_j9hSQ0?si=6_hPMafgTiD53s72; The merchant, https://youtu.be/fcfTbklepv8?si=XZhHMPhkA2E1t3E8.Source dataDuring the expansion phase (1200–1315) the Sound fishery for western Baltic herring emerged. At the end of the thirteenth century, catches from this relatively small area dominated the whole western Baltic herring production3. A first maximum of catches was reached around 1300, with 23,000 t. The expansion of the fishery is in line with an increase in demand4 and favourable economic conditions, as high-quality salt from saltworks in northern Germany became more easily available as a main production factor5.In the stagnation phase (1315–1520), the economy was stagnant: agricultural output declined as temperatures had decreased and stayed low, leading to famines6 (1315–1322). Moreover, Europe was hit hard by the Bubonic plague around 1350, which killed 25–35% of the population7. This decimated the workforce of fisheries as well8. In the fifteenth century, climate conditions were variable but the economy remained stagnant, mainly because of deflation caused by a lack of bullion (gold and silver). Money ran short9. Additionally, a series of wars in the Baltic region hindered herring catch and trade. Total output amounted to 19,000–23,000 t during this period.When the fishery reached its boom phase (1520–1570), the crisis of the Late Middle Ages was overcome: the population size recovered and an influx of gold and silver provided the economy with new momentum9. Acreage was enlarged6 and the herring market expanded. Still, in the first two decades of the sixteenth century the Sound fishery could not benefit from general economic growth. Danish wars hindered its expansion. Finally, under the reign of Frederic I (1523–1533), trade improved3,10. Average outputs of the Scanian fishery amounted to about 55,000 t between 1524 and 1570, with catches reaching up to 75,000 t in some years.The collapse of the Sound fishery began in the 1570s. Skanor and Falsterbo suffered from shifting dunes, destroying the economic infrastructure (a phenomenon linked to climatic changes at that time11). In the 1580s, appearance of herring shoals increasingly fluctuated in the Sound3,12. Temperatures were falling again13. Fishermen emigrated to Bohuslän, a Swedish province on the northernmost part of the west coast of the present country, where herring harvest was booming in the 1580s14. The situation worsened as nobility enforced serfdom (clod duty) in the early seventeenth century, barring peasants from leaving their landlord’s grounds in autumn to fish, which massively limited the available workforce. Demand for herring shifted to imported, cheap and presumably larger North Sea herring, provided by an uprising fishery. Considering the number of fishers taxed in Kronborg Len (North Zealand) in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries15, the yields of the Sound fishery (after a meantime rise in the 1620s) must have dropped to an average of 1,000 t per year.It took until the 1950s for outputs to reach medieval levels again16. In this paper, we investigate the particular roles that overfishing, climate and socioeconomic factors played in this sudden collapse of the Baltic herring fishery in the sixteenth century, drivers that also have relevance for many fisheries today.Shortly before the collapse of the fishery, catch quantities reached >70,000 t in certain years. To evaluate the potential harmfulness of historic catch quantities on the autumn-spawning herring stock, we need to estimate the corresponding stock size.Herring stock productivity and hence catch potential is influenced by climatic conditions, for example temperature. Autumn-spawning herring is considered sensible against harsh winter conditions17. In the period under consideration, climate cooling had the potential to limit autumn-spawning herring stock growth, as a period of regional cooling, particularly pronounced in the North Atlantic region18 and known as Little Ice Age, started19. The herring fishery was (and still is) embedded in a complex socioecological network and was therefore also affected by socioeconomic factors, for example those influencing fish demand or larger-scale production conditions such as wars in the area. We collected a wealth of socioeconomic context data to evaluate the importance of these factors potentially acting in synergy or counteracting climate and stock dynamics.Our approach builds on a long tradition of bioeconomic modelling of renewable resources, which has demonstrated how interactions between resource dynamics and human exploitation can generate nonlinear outcomes, including overexploitation, collapse and regime shifts in fisheries and socioecological systems (for example, refs. 20,21,22). Conceptually related models, sharing a common analytical structure that links ecological dynamics with economic drivers, have also been applied to broader historical cases of resource use and societal development (for example, Pleistocene megafauna extinction23). However, empirical applications of such frameworks to long-term, data-constrained historical fisheries remain rare, particularly where quantitative reconstruction and system-level analysis are combined.Here we first estimate historic sustainable fishing limits as well as stock depletion rates (biomass relative to carrying capacity), using a bioeconomic stock assessment (BESA) method based on catch and price data time series. This allows us to test the hypothesis that a stock collapse caused the breakdown of the fishery. Then, we construct a qualitative model of the fishery system and evaluate its dynamic behaviour using loop analysis. Thereby, we identify which forcing factors were most important in determining fishery outputs during different phases and that finally caused the collapse of the fishery. Our analysis highlights that proper management of natural resources cannot be achieved without considering environmental conditions as well as the human components of the system.ResultsSustainable fishing limits and stock depletion ratesApplying a BESA tool24, we estimated sustainable fishing limits (estimates of maximum sustainable yield, MSY) for the different phases of the fishery (Fig. 2). BESA exploits information on the variation of catch and price data over time and assumes that rents are driven to zero, as is classic for an unregulated fishery. We further assume that this happens rapidly at each point in time, considering the fishery as one with a high speed of adjustment. Each of the four price data time series yielded an estimate of sustainable fishing limits, compared with realized catches across phases of the fishery. During the expansion and stagnation periods, realized catches were well below sustainable fishing limits (Fig. 2a,b). The boom period of the fishery (Fig. 2c), however, is characterized by overfishing of the resource. The catches during this phase would not have been sustainable over longer periods. After the collapse of the fishery, catches were well below estimates of MSY (Fig. 2d). The time series of estimated stock depletion rates (biomass relative to carrying capacity) (Fig. 2e) show an initial decrease of the stock during the expansion phase. We find that stock size substantially increased between 1400 and 1500 during the stagnation period. This holds true for all investigated models (Supplementary Fig. 2). Stock size decreased from around 1510 onwards (exact onset depending on the price data series used; Supplementary Fig. 2). During the boom phase of the fishery, this decrease is quite substantial (reduction to 41–51% of maximum observed biomass), but there is no indication of a collapse of the stock. As expected, BESA results indicate that stock productivity changed over time and was significantly associated with climatic conditions.                   (1)
                  
                    Expansion (1200–1315): The climate is cooling, although starting from a relatively high level.                   (2)

                  (3)
                  
                    Boom phase (1520–1570): Climate is warming. The economy is boosting, among others factors because of the influx of noble metal. Finally, wars in the Baltic region end.               Our main interest was to identify the reasons for the sudden collapse of the fishery. As data availability was especially low after the collapse, we omitted the low catch period 1600–1650 from this part of the analysis. Loop analysis was used to assess how perturbations that alter the growth rate of individual variables affect system dynamics and their cumulative impacts. We applied this approach to test whether factors influencing the socioecological system could reproduce the herring stock and harvest responses estimated with BESA across the four phases of the time series. Results are reported in the table of predictions (Fig. 3b), which shows how a positive perturbation of each variable in the rows influences the others in the columns. Clustering along rows identifies variables with comparable system-level impacts and grouping along columns reveals similarities in response patterns.Herring stock (HS), herring harvest (HA), workforce (WF) and demand (DE) cluster together as factors that, if perturbed (that is, row direction), result in similar responses at the whole-system level. A second cluster groups population size (PO), state of the economy (EC) and agriculture (AG), which are socioeconomic factors with similar impacts on the system, usually under-represented in bioeconomic models. The influence of AG on the system deviates slightly from the consistent pattern observed for EC and PO: an increase in AG growth rate in fact reduces the demand for herring (DE), whereas herring stock (HS) decreases only mildly and herring harvest (HA) increases slightly. Finally, climate cooling (CC) and war (WA) represent large-scale factors outside regional control. Climate cooling exerts a complex response. Although colder years directly reduce herring stock, indirect positive effects could partly offset this impact and even yield a slight net increase in stock size (Supplementary Table 3). Therefore, the network architecture can account for a net negative response of the herring stock to climate cooling, but only if the direct effect outweighs the longer chains transmitting positive signals.The major dynamics of the catch time series are reproduced by our model when the assumed press perturbations are applied (Table 2). First, we observed a clear chance of increase in harvest during the expansion period (1200–1315). Second, a slight tendency towards decreased herring harvest during the stagnation period (1315–1520) was found, which is followed by a strong likelihood of increase during the boom phase (1520–1570). Finally, our predictions combine for an unambiguous signal in the fourth phase, which points towards a very likely, strong decrease in harvest, that is a fishery collapse (1570–1600).Table 2 Overall loop analysis predictions for HA in the four phases of the time series, resulting from press perturbations on selected variablesFull size tableClimate cooling by itself cannot explain the dynamics of the fishery, especially if we assume that the same magnitude of impacts is transmitted across chains of all lengths (Supplementary Table 3). For example, climate cooling also affected agriculture adversely and the associated decline in population reduced the workforce for fishing. Instead, the interplay of ecological, economic and social factors is needed to reconstruct and understand the system reaction. Furthermore, it is a combination of local- (workforce), regional- (economy and demand) and large-scale factors (climate cooling and war), which determined the fate of this fishery (Table 2).DiscussionThe reconstructed time series of western Baltic autumn-spawning herring catches from 1200 to 1650 showed distinct dynamics. Stock assessment results in combination with loop analysis suggested that the collapse of the fishery was caused by a combination of climate change, overfishing and socioeconomic factors. This closely resembles the situation today of western Baltic spring-spawning herring fisheries.Direct data on the yields of Sound fishery (toll books and chronicles) are sparse, making the construction of a Baltic herring catch time series more challenging than for the better-documented North Sea herring fisheries (1600–1850)2,4. Hence, the question as to whether the collapse of Sound fishery was caused by overfishing remained unanswered4. Although direct data are lacking, demographic, economic, climate and political history provide a wealth of contextual factors (prices, market-volumes and legal framework), which was harnessed only rudimentarily15,28. We validated historic records and filled gaps by projections, considering the availability of salt as the main production factor for the ‘herring industry’. Combining all available information yielded a catch-data time series, which mirrors the major dynamics of the fishery. Data density is highest during the boom phase and the onset of the collapse, when yearly estimates can be provided1.For most periods, continuous direct records did not exist (see Supplementary Information for a detailed description of time-series construction), so the series was built through extrapolation and interpolation linked primarily to production-related proxies, most notably salt availability and salt prices and to environmental indicators; broader socioeconomic variables (for example, demographic trends and general economic conditions) served only as contextual consistency checks, not as quantitative inputs. This distinction matters for avoiding circularity: the reconstruction is constrained by direct trade records and material production factors, whereas the socioeconomic variables analysed in the loop analysis (population, demand, economy and workforce) are treated as external drivers not quantitatively embedded in the reconstruction, allowing the subsequent analyses to evaluate their influence on temporal variation independently. Plausibility was checked against constraints on production (salt and labour availability, legal frameworks, fishing technology and market demand) and ecological conditions (spawning season, fish size and age structure); estimates were deliberately conservative, with adjustments for unregistered catches, subsistence consumption and double counting of kongekøb quantities. Certainty varies considerably over time: relatively robust figures exist for some years in the late fourteenth and early sixteenth centuries, whereas thirteenth- and early-fourteenth-century yields are inferred indirectly from salt production and demographic proxies and the post-1570s decline relies on sparse tax records and comparisons with other fisheries. The final output is therefore not a precise year-by-year dataset but a smoothed trend curve for 1200–1650 synthesizing fragmentary evidence at varying confidence levels; still, the major dynamics underlying our analysis are well documented and beyond doubt.Initially, there had been some indications of overfishing and a subsequent stock collapse as the cause of the fishery breakdown. The average size of herring caught declined. On the basis of processing information, the average weight of an individual herring was 82 g (in around 1400). In 1485, it temporarily dropped to 67 g. In the Viking Ages (around 900), average herring caught reached a length of 26 cm, making a weight of 154 g (ref. 1). Because of an expanding ‘fish industry’, its weight halved; that is, herring was caught about 3–4 years younger (assuming there was not a change in growth rate). Contemporaries seem to have been aware of the problem early on: pelagic trawl nets were prohibited in 13713 and there are indications that net mesh-size was regulated (1386). Our analysis confirms findings from ref. 29 that catches of autumn-spawning herring amounted to between 10,000 and 50,000 t during the period considered in our analysis. However, they also show that the western Baltic autumn-spawning herring stock did not collapse in the second half of the sixteenth century29. Using ancient DNA and genomics, they conclude that the fishery had a negative impact, but that population dynamics were consistent with environmental change. The herring stock declined, but this was not the only reason for the collapse of the fishery. Excessive fish extraction caused the stock to shrink. Smaller stock size most probably exacerbated the exposure of these autumn spawners to the unfavourably cooler climate30,31, which lowered the herring stock productivity.During several phases of our time series, environmental change (that is, climate cooling) negatively affected the herring stock productivity. Temperature is known to strongly affect many fish populations32,33, including herring34,35 and low temperatures negatively affect herring stock productivity in autumn spawners, including in the Baltic Sea6,36. In contrast to historic times, in recent years the role of climate warming for stock dynamics has been the focus of many studies, including western Baltic spring-spawning herring37. The drastic, complete breakdown of this important fishery dependent on autumn spawners can, however, only be understood as an interplay of overfishing, climate, social factors and economy (Fig. 4). The overall negative effect of cooling phases on the western Baltic autumn-spawning herring stock is justified only if the magnitudes of their direct impacts outweigh those transmitted through long, indirect pathways (Supplementary Table 3).Fig. 4: Conceptual representation of major press perturbations influencing the western Baltic autumn-spawning herring fishery.Full size imageTrends of such perturbations have been grouped to climate, social and economic. Changepoints in fishery dynamics (tipping points) are indicated together with important context data.Climate effects refer to the direct impact on herring stock dynamics, but the loop model explicitly captures how cooling/warming events can be mediated by socioeconomic variables, an outcome that may challenge intuitive cause–effect interpretations. Over centuries, the major pressures partly offset each other, leading to relatively moderate changes in catch quantity (Table 2, upper two rows). At the beginning of the sixteenth century, all pressures suddenly became reinforcing, promoting a boost of the fishery (Table 2, second last row). In the middle of the sixteenth century, the situation reversed and climate, social, economic and fishery pressures influenced the fishery negatively, resulting in its collapse (Table 2, last row). Loop model predictions allow clustering system variables based on the way they respond to disturbance (columns in Fig. 3b). Herring harvest is close to local (workforce) and regional (economy, agriculture and population size) socioeconomic factors whereas the biological component (herring stock) clusters together with a large-scale factor such as war. This outcome highlights that proper management of natural resources cannot be achieved without considering the human components of the system.Our results are consistent with core insights from bioeconomic theory, which predict that renewable resource systems can exhibit nonlinear dynamics arising from feedbacks between ecological processes and human behaviour. In particular, the combination of increasing exploitation pressure, changing environmental conditions and evolving socioeconomic drivers observed here aligns with theoretical expectations of overexploitation and regime shifts in coupled human–natural systems, for example refs. 20,21. The absence of a complete biological stock collapse, despite the breakdown of the fishery, further supports the idea that economic viability and ecological sustainability may diverge over time, as highlighted in previous bioeconomic studies. More broadly, our findings resonate with theoretical and empirical work on long-term resource use in human societies, where models of coupled population-resource dynamics show that even simple feedback structures can produce collapse or transition dynamics when external pressures or internal thresholds are crossed23,38. The western Baltic herring fishery provides a rare empirical example over several centuries that supports these general insights, while also demonstrating how several drivers such as climate variability, economic incentives or institutional constraints, interact to shape outcomes in real-world systems.Our analysis gains practical relevance for management today by lending support to an ecosystem-based fisheries management approach. We show that the collapse of a fishery can significantly be triggered by socioeconomic pressures. Any effort to guide fisheries towards a sustainable future amid global change will therefore need to include socioeconomic considerations. An illustrative example is the present western Baltic spring-spawning herring fishery, which is now outside safe biological limits39 and on the brink of collapse. This fishery targets spring-spawning herring, unlike the autumn spawners of medieval times. The stock size has decreased drastically and, accordingly, there has been a ‘zero catch’ advice39. Stock decline has been driven by overfishing40,41. The population is now so depleted that recovery is constrained by unfavourable environmental conditions (for example, climate-driven negative effects on recruitment37) and food web interactions that, together with residual fishing, prevent any surplus production. In the absence of fishing mortality, however, the stock would probably still cope with these other stressors and recover. Herring fisheries have long been an important part of coastal economies, societies and cultural heritage. Preventing this looming collapse is therefore of high societal interest and a severe challenge for fisheries management. While recovery of the resource stock remains the prime target, (national) management measures increasingly also address socioeconomic pressures on the stock and the fishery, as now discussed in high-level political groups in Denmark and Germany. Consequently, the recently published report of the German Commission on the Future of Baltic Sea Fisheries42 suggests measures to improve socioeconomic framework conditions, for example infrastructure and diversification. Management will need to include socioeconomic considerations, if truly sustainable fisheries and optimal outcomes, are to be achieved. This is the lesson learnt from history as described here.MethodsClimate forcingInformation on medieval climate anomaly is based on a climate field reconstruction approach by ref. 13. To impute a yearly temperature anomaly time series, we used the data provided for specific years and imposed a linear interpolation function (na_interpolation) from the R package imputeTS43. The linear interpolation resulted in a time series with ‘hard corners’ based on the original data. Therefore, we used the smooth.spline function from R44 to fit a cubic smoothing spline to the imputed data with a smoothing parameter of 0.3. As we assumed that climate conditions impacted herring productivity, we further included temperature anomalies as a factor in the BESA analysis.Estimation of sustainable fishing limitsWe used a newly developed BESA24 to evaluate sustainable fishing limits of the herring stock over time, based on catch data and available price time series. BESA assumes that the herring stock was fished under open access conditions, where fishers could freely enter and exit the fishery and each year will do so until profits are driven to zero. It then exploits variation in prices, which stems for example from demand shocks, varying market conditions and changes in the supply of elsewhere-sourced herring, and which would have induced the Baltic Sea herring fishers to adapt their fishing effort as a result of the open access nature of the fishery. Normally, price data time series need to be corrected for potential deflation before being used in BESA. In this special historic case, it was not possible to achieve a meaningful correction. Therefore, results have to be treated with caution. Moreover, BESA accounts for stock-dependent harvesting costs, meaning that, all else being equal, the cost of harvesting a unit of fish increases as stock size declines. Given these assumptions, BESA then relies on a state–space model combined with an extended Kalman filter and can identify through Bayesian estimation the time series of MSY levels, stock biomass, the natural growth rate, carrying capacity as well as the cost parameter on the economic side.We combined annual herring harvest data with four decadal price time series from major herring markets that contained sufficient observations of salted herring prices overlapping with the harvest records, namely in England (1270–1600), Hamburg (Germany, 1450–1600), Brabant (1390–1600) and Utrecht (1420–1600) (the last two, located in present-day Netherlands), as compiled by ref. 1. We estimated the climate impact as a quadratic effect of the climate anomaly on the natural growth rate of the stock (Supplementary Fig. 3). Supplementary Information, section 2 gives details on model, estimation, results, diagnostics and robustness checks.Loop analysis to identify the key drivers of system dynamicsLoop analysis makes predictions for the dynamic behaviour of complex systems starting from simple information such as presence/absence of interactions and their signs. Hence, it does not require knowing the form of the equations that describe the relationships between variables, it is not constrained by the need for using the same units and the user does not have to quantify interaction strengths45. The catch time series used in BESA is independent of the socioeconomic variables included in the loop analysis, as these variables were not used as quantitative predictors during the reconstruction procedure. The signed digraph used in loop analysis depicts interactions between pairs of variables (nodes) and informs on the sign of each relationship (link), distinguishing between positive (+) and negative (−). To execute the loop analysis, the signed digraph has to be converted into a square Jacobian matrix where each link is represented by a non-zero element of absolute value equal to 1, indicating either a positive or a negative direct effect of the row variable on the column variable. Loop analysis predicts the direction of change of variables (for example, ‘herring harvest’) in response to press perturbations, that is sustained external inputs acting on the rate of change of other variables46. Here one such press perturbation is climate cooling. The output is the table of predictions, which summarizes the net, cumulative impact that an increase in the growth rate of the row variable has on the column variables. Such a net impact is obtained by combining the effects that travel through the direct connection and all indirect pathways linking each pair of variables45. Prediction values range between −100% and +100% and represent the relative frequency of negative or positive responses across simulation runs, rather than quantitative changes in variable magnitude. They therefore indicate the certainty of the direction of change, but not its intensity. To generate these predictions, interaction strengths were randomly varied across simulations while preserving the sign structure of the network and only stable matrices were retained. Determining the timing of shifts in conditions and system responses is inherently challenging. The asynchronous occurrence of perturbations, together with lags in the propagation of indirect effects, complicates the evaluation of net impacts on response variables. To address this, we focus on four extended intervals, the shortest spanning 50 years (the boom phase, 1520–1570), and integrate the effects of perturbations over each interval, rather than resolving fine-scale dynamics. Besides predicting the consequences that press perturbations have on the entire system, loop analysis allows clustering the variables; here we grouped variables according to the scores reported in the table of predictions, using the Manhattan distance (R function dist). Clustering along the rows groups variables whose perturbation leads to comparable overall responses patterns across all other system variables, considering both the sequence of signs and their relative intensity along the entire row. Because each variable also responds to perturbations affecting itself through self-loops and indirect feedback pathways, self-responses are included in the table of predictions. Clustering along the columns, in turn, groups variables that show similar response patterns when compared across all possible perturbations applied to the system. In the dendrograms, branch lengths reflect the degree of dissimilarity between clusters, with longer branches indicating greater differences; the ordering of variables along the axes is determined by the hierarchical clustering so that more similar variables are placed closer together. Further details about the algorithm and the R script for its execution are found in ref. 47. items.title: Buon compleanno, Macchiagrande!
items.description: Celebrati i 60 anni del WWF Italia, i 40 anni della gestione WWF dell'Oasi di Macchiagrande i 30 anni della Riserva Naturale Statale del Litorale Roma
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie L’Oasi WWF compie 40 anni Una giornata dedicata alla natura, ad una storia di visioni e alle sfide future della conservazione dell’ambiente ha riunito a Maccarese Fiumicino, istituzioni e realtà del territorio in occasione di tre importanti ricorrenze: i 60 anni dalla nascita del WWF Italia, i 40 anni dall’avvio della gestione WWF dell’Oasi di Macchiagrande, di proprietà di Maccarese S.p.A. Società Agricola Benefit e i 30 anni dall’istituzione della Riserva Naturale Statale del Litorale Romano.La mattinata, ospitata presso il Castello San Giorgio, ha visto la partecipazione di quasi 250 alunni delle scuole primarie del Comune di Fiumicino, che hanno sperimentato laboratori e percorsi dedicati alla scoperta della biodiversità e degli ecosistemi della Riserva grazie alle guide esperte del WWF e della Maccarese S.p.A, . Confronto tra istituzioni, con il Presidente WWF Italia Nel pomeriggio si è svolto un confronto tra le istituzioni dedicato alla storia della tutela ambientale nel territorio di Maccarese e alle prospettive future della Riserva e dell’Oasi WWF di Macchiagrande, condotto da Francesco Marcone, Responsabile Conservazione Oasi WWF Italia. “Le celebrazioni di oggi non rappresentano soltanto un momento di ricordo di ciò che è stato fatto negli ultimi decenni, ma soprattutto un’occasione per costruire una visione condivisa del futuro”, ha dichiarato Francesco Marcone, WWF Italia. “L’esperienza di Macchiagrande dimostra come la collaborazione tra proprietari, associazioni, istituzioni e cittadini possa produrre risultati concreti per la conservazione della natura. Ringrazio la Maccarese e l’AD Claudio Destro per la rinnovata fiducia riposta in tutti questi anni”.All’incontro hanno partecipato Claudio Destro, Amministratore Delegato di Maccarese S.p.A. Società Agricola Benefit, Luciano Di Tizio, Presidente del WWF Italia, Mario Baccini, Sindaco di Fiumicino, Romeo De Angelis, Presidente della Riserva Naturale Statale del Litorale Romano, Ezio Di Genesio Pagliuca, Consigliere comunale di Fiumicino, e Giulia Bonella, Direttrice della Tenuta Presidenziale di Castelporziano. Uno scorcio dell’Oasi di Macchiagrande Dal confronto è emersa la volontà di consolidare le collaborazioni tra enti gestori, amministrazioni, proprietari delle aree, mondo della ricerca e associazioni ambientaliste, al fine ad approfondire, con un approccio scientifico e partecipato, le principali criticità ambientali che interessano il territorio e a individuare le migliori strategie di gestione e conservazione.“L’Oasi di Macchiagrande rappresenta una delle esperienze più significative della storia del WWF in Italia e racconta l’evoluzione del nostro impegno per la tutela della biodiversità”, ha dichiarato Luciano Di Tizio, Presidente del WWF Italia. “Sessant’anni di WWF ci insegnano che i risultati più importanti si ottengono quando le istituzioni, il mondo scientifico, le imprese e le comunità locali lavorano insieme. Le sfide ambientali che abbiamo di fronte, dai cambiamenti climatici alla gestione degli ecosistemi forestali, richiedono responsabilità condivisa, conoscenza e capacità di fare rete. Macchiagrande e la Riserva del Litorale Romano possono continuare a essere un laboratorio di buone pratiche per tutto il Paese.” La giornata si è conclusa con l’intervento di Francesco Petretti, divulgatore scientifico, storico conoscitore del territorio e tra i protagonisti dell’istituzione dell’Oasi WWF di Macchiagrande.Le tre ricorrenze celebrano un patrimonio costruito in decenni di lavoro, ma soprattutto rilanciano un impegno comune verso il futuro: promuovere educazione ambientale, ricerca scientifica e collaborazione tra tutti gli attori del territorio per garantire la tutela e la valorizzazione della Riserva Naturale Statale del Litorale Romano e dell’Oasi WWF di Macchiagrande. Macchiagrande, Foce dell’Arrone e Vasche di Maccarese Con i suoi ambienti di duna sabbiosa litoranea e un bellissimo bosco mediterraneo, l’Oasi WWF di Macchiagrande rappresenta una delle aree protette di maggior valore ambientale del litorale laziale. items.title: Ue, il 91% delle aziende considera la transizione verde un motore di competitività
items.description:
I dati della nuova indagine “Beyond Uncertainty”, realizzata da GlobeScan e commissionata dal WWF
The post Ue, il 91% delle aziende considera la trans
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie L’idea che l’Unione europea debba indebolire le norme ambientali per restare competitiva non trova riscontro tra le imprese europee. È quanto emerge dalla nuova indagine “Beyond Uncertainty”, realizzata da GlobeScan e commissionata dal WWF, che raccoglie le opinioni di 350 dirigenti d’impresa operanti in diversi settori dell’economia europea. Al contrario, 9 dirigenti aziendali su 10 (91%) ritengono che la transizione verde rafforzi la competitività dell’Unione europea nel lungo periodo. Inoltre, oltre la metà degli intervistati (55%) afferma che i recenti sforzi dell’UE per la “semplificazione” normativa hanno avuto un impatto negativo o misto sulla propria attività. Una distanza tra l’UE e le richieste delle imprese I risultati evidenziano una netta distanza tra la spinta attuale dell’Unione europea ad allentare le normative ambientali e di sostenibilità e ciò che le aziende dichiarano di aver bisogno per competere maggiormente. Per i leader aziendali intervistati, dare continuità alla transizione verde europea rappresenta una priorità economica: significa ridurre l’esposizione ai rischi climatici e a quelli generati dalla perdita di biodiversità, rafforzare la sicurezza energetica e dell’approvvigionamento delle risorse e garantire maggiore stabilità dei costi. L’estate appena trascorsa è stata un doloroso promemoria del fatto che l’Europa sta già pagando il prezzo della crisi climatica, con enormi costi economici. Eppure la risposta dell’Unione europea è ridurre e indebolire le norme di tutela ambientale. Le imprese ci stanno dicendo chiaramente che indebolire le politiche di sostenibilità renderà l’Europa meno competitiva”, dichiara Ester Asin, Direttrice dell’Ufficio europeo del WWF. I costi economici dell’inazione climatica si fanno già sentire I costi economici dell’inazione climatica stanno già colpendo l’Europa. Il caldo estremo registrato quest’estate potrebbe ridurre il PIL dell’UE di circa l’1% nel 2026 a causa dei danni economici provocati. Allo stesso tempo, la Commissione europea stima che il costo derivante dalla mancata attuazione delle attuali normative ambientali dell’Unione europea ammonti a circa 180 miliardi di euro all’anno, una cifra dieci volte superiore ai 17 miliardi di euro di risparmi amministrativi annuali che, sempre secondo la Commissione, sarebbero stati ottenuti finora attraverso gli interventi di semplificazione. L’indagine rileva inoltre che i recenti tentativi di riaprire e rivedere la legislazione ambientale europea stanno generando incertezza per molte aziende: solo il 29% dei dirigenti aziendali afferma infatti di aver riscontrato effetti positivi derivanti dalle recenti iniziative dell’UE volte a semplificare le norme. Tra coloro che riportano impatti negativi o misti, la conseguenza più citata è la maggiore incertezza sulla futura direzione delle politiche europee (57%), insieme agli investimenti già sostenuti per adeguarsi alla normativa europea e resi parzialmente inutili dalle successive modifiche normative. Alla domanda su quali dovrebbero essere le priorità dell’UE per rafforzare la competitività, le imprese collocano al primo posto politiche e normative prevedibili e coerenti (43%), davanti agli investimenti pubblici e agli incentivi (31%) e all’energia pulita a prezzi accessibili (29%). “I leader aziendali non chiedono ai decisori politici europei di scegliere tra sostenibilità e competitività, ed è arrivato il momento di abbandonare questa contrapposizione fuorviante. Chiedono invece regole europee ambiziose e stabili che diano alle imprese la fiducia necessaria per investire e innovare. Il vero costo economico deriva dal ritardare la transizione verde e dal creare incertezza sulla sua direzione” conclude Ester Asin. items.title: Il metodo scientifico contro il negazionismo climatico
items.description: Il consenso scientifico sul ruolo umano nel riscaldamento globale nasce da oltre un secolo di ricerca e confronto tra ipotesi alternative. Il metodo s
items.body:
Il metodo scientifico contro il negazionismo climatico                
												
																																	                
					Set 14, 2026Set 15, 20262 commenti su Il metodo scientifico contro il negazionismo climatico

Il consenso scientifico sul ruolo umano nel riscaldamento globale nasce da oltre un secolo di ricerca e confronto tra ipotesi alternative. Il metodo scientifico non richiede che ogni teoria venga discussa all’infinito: quelle smentite dai dati vengono progressivamente abbandonate.

Anche le spiegazioni alternative del riscaldamento attuale sono state studiate, senza trovare evidenze sufficienti a sostenerle. Il confronto avviene attraverso la ricerca pubblicata a valle della revisione tra pari. Considerare accertata l’origine antropica del riscaldamento globale è quindi il risultato del metodo scientifico, non la sua negazione.

Peraltro, in questo caso non si tratta di un semplice dibattito scientifico fine a sé stesso, bensì di qualcosa che sottende una serie di azioni di mitigazione che devono essere messe in campo al più presto, senza ulteriori tentennamenti.

Al di là degli errori marchiani nei grafici di Franco Battaglia pubblicati su La Verità (si vedano i precedenti post qui e qui), l’articolo pubblicato il 2 agosto contiene altre affermazioni gravi che purtroppo spesso si sentono nel dibattito sul clima.

Battaglia ha accusato due fisici e climatologi, Bruno Carli e Filippo Giorgi, di non seguire il metodo scientifico, in quanto hanno dichiarato inequivocabile il ruolo antropico sull’attuale cambiamento climatico, hanno citato i rapporti dell’IPCC, e hanno sostenuto che è chiuso il dibattito sulle cause delle variazioni climatiche attuali. La comunità scientifica, secondo Battaglia, rinnegherebbe in questo modo il metodo galileiano perché rifiuterebbe di confrontarsi in dibattiti pubblici con chi nega le cause umane, e pertanto non conoscerebbe le critiche che questi muoverebbero.

In realtà il dibattito sulle cause del riscaldamento globale è veramente chiuso, e ci sono anche molti altri campi della scienza in cui lo è. Praticamente nessuno dubita che molte malattie siano dovute ad infezioni batteriche o virali, che la radioattività sia dovuta a decadimenti nel nucleo dell’atomo, che la gravità sia dovuta alle deformazioni dello spaziotempo descritte dalla relatività generale, che gli organismi viventi cambino nel tempo soggetti ai meccanismi dell’evoluzione descritti da Charles Darwin, che la Terra abbia circa 4,7 miliardi di anni, che i continenti si muovano secondo la tettonica a zolle, che l’Universo sia in espansione. In tutte queste affermazioni ci sono punti oscuri, cose che possono lasciare qualche appiglio a chi voglia proporre alternative. La relatività generale potrebbe essere sostituita da teorie più ampie, l’evoluzione darwiniana potrebbe essere integrata da altri meccanismi, ma il quadro generale difficilmente cambierà. Questo significa che un astrofisico che consideri “chiuso” il dibattito sull’espansione dell’Universo stia rigettando il metodo scientifico? Che non conosca le teorie alternative proposte? In realtà queste teorie trovano spazio nelle riviste del settore, ma semplicemente non riescono a convincere se non una ristrettissima minoranza dei ricercatori, oltre ad essere spesso pure in contrasto tra di loro.

In effetti il cuore della mentalità scientifica è la libertà di pensarla diversamente, di esplorare strade nuove, di proporre visioni alternative. Ogni volta che si apre un problema scientifico emergono voci discordanti e ogni scienziato esplora quella per lui più promettente. Molti ricercatori si accodano a quelle più gettonate, ma altri sanno benissimo che il loro successo dipende dalla capacità di smentire la visione in quel momento dominante e proporne una migliore. Ma via via che le ricerche proseguono, alcuni rami vengono tagliati. Ci si accorge che non portano da nessuna parte, che le premesse non erano corrette, e soprattutto che le ipotesi non reggono alla prova dei fatti. Il consenso si forma in questo modo, per eliminazione di tante ipotesi logiche, magari plausibili, ma purtroppo sbagliate.

C’è sempre la possibilità che emerga una nuova ipotesi che spieghi meglio i fatti, succede: ma man mano che la teoria si afferma, questo diventa però sempre più difficile e più raro. La teoria rimasta ha assorbito parte di quelle concorrenti, ha eliminato, grazie anche alle loro critiche, alcuni aspetti sbagliati, e finisce per coprire un ambito molto più vasto di quello del problema originale, per cui ogni nuova teoria si troverà a dover spiegare un insieme di fenomeni molto grande in modo altrettanto accurato.

Negli esempi fatti, come per l’origine antropica dell’attuale cambiamento climatico, il dibattito c’è già stato, e dopo oltre un secolo di fuoco incrociato queste teorie hanno una solidità che richiede argomentazioni molto forti, e dati che oggi semplicemente non esistono, per essere contestate. In futuro potranno emergere nuove evidenze, e il dibattito si riaprirà. Non oggi. E molto difficilmente alcune conclusioni di base, come appunto l’origine antropica del riscaldamento globale, verranno modificate, in quanto sostenute da una conoscenza solida della fisica del clima alla base e da una quantità di dati immensa che conferma la teoria. Ogni teoria alternativa avrebbe quindi il problema di dover incorporare anche questi dati e queste evidenze. Ogni solida teoria, anche quelle citate sopra, avrà comunque sempre qualche rompiscatole irriducibile, che continuerà a cercare di scovare ed evidenziare punti deboli. E per fortuna i rompiscatole esistono, perché i punti deboli li vedi male dall’interno, e l’evidenziarli ha consentito alle teorie di raffinarsi, correggere errori, e diventare più solide.

Un esempio classico, per tornare al clima, è l’ipotesi avanzata dall’astrofisico Svensmark, di un influsso sul clima dei raggi cosmici. Un maggior flusso di particelle cariche, non schermate dal vento solare, potrebbe favorire la formazione di nuvole, alterando la quantità di radiazione solare che queste riflettono. I dati che Svensmark portava indicavano questa possibilità, che venne presa seriamente in considerazione, al punto che il CERN mise in piedi un esperimento dedicato, in cui raggi cosmici artificiali interagivano con nubi artificiali in una grande camera, per studiare il fenomeno. Abbiamo imparato diverse cose, ma l’ipotesi originale è stata smentita. Nel frattempo, la correlazione trovata da Svensmark tra flusso di raggi cosmici e nubi è stata pure smentita da nuovi dati. Questo non ha convinto l’astrofisico, che continua a sostenere la sua ipotesi, ma ha convinto tutti gli altri. Il dibattito su questo punto si è dunque chiuso.

In ogni caso il dibattito scientifico non si fa sui quotidiani o nelle conferenze pubbliche. La scienza si fa su riviste “peer reviewed” (ovvero soggette a revisione tra pari), in cui esporre le proprie ipotesi e presentare i propri dati. Per pubblicare occorre tuttavia passare un filtro, dei colleghi cercheranno di valutare la correttezza formale dell’articolo proposto, se i dati supportano le conclusioni; ad esempio, usare un grafico fermo al 1855 su scala locale, per sostenere che nel 2000 non ci sia stato un aumento di temperatura globale particolarmente rilevante, non verrebbe accettato, sarebbe rigettato senza pietà. Anche la riproposizione di argomenti già presentati e ripresentati non è sufficiente alla pubblicazione, servono argomenti nuovi. Non si tratta di una censura contro le idee innovative, anche perché con l’elevato numero di riviste scientifiche esistenti sarebbe praticamente impossibile imporla. Semmai esiste il problema opposto: oggi diverse riviste accettano per la pubblicazione, a pagamento, anche articoli di qualità molto scadente.

Alla fine, gli articoli che criticano l’origine umana del riscaldamento globale sono pochissimi, tra quelli recenti circa 1 ogni 200 che invece lo sostengono, un centinaio in tutto tra gli 88 mila articoli di climatologia pubblicati nell’ultimo decennio, ma proprio per quello non passano inosservati. Qualsiasi climatologo conosce molto bene quelli che per Battaglia sarebbero “i fatti che lo sconfessano”. Nei post di Climalteranti molti di questi sono già stati discussi. Esistono in rete siti dedicati in cui ciascuno di questi “fatti” viene analizzato, ed è possibile esaminare le argomentazioni e gli articoli scientifici pro e contro. Insomma, il dibattito è chiuso perché le argomentazioni sono state prese in considerazione, analizzate, e rigettate in base ai dati disponibili.

Le cose vanno molto peggio per chi opera ormai fuori dal mondo accademico, come Franco Battaglia, che sostiene che il riscaldamento in atto non abbia un’origine antropica riproponendo grafici fermi al 1850, curve di assorbimento interpretate male, grafici che mostrano un aumento della temperatura per sostenere che questo aumento non ci sia, calcoli sballati di equilibrio radiativo, errori marchiani di calcolo, e tanti altri dati sbagliati e fraintendimenti di cui solo in parte abbiamo avuto tempo (e voglia) di occuparci in queste pagine.

Infine, poco sensate sono anche le accuse all’IPCC, che certamente segue il metodo galileiano. È un organismo che passa in rassegna le conclusioni di tutti gli articoli, anche di quell’1 su 200 contrario, e cerca di sintetizzare le conclusioni. Anzi, lavorando su un consenso, dà un peso molto maggiore a chi è più prudente relativamente agli impatti degli scenari futuri, si presentano solo gli effetti che sostanzialmente tutti ritengono realistico aspettarci. Ma essere galileiani non significa dare lo stesso peso al geocentrismo rispetto all’eliocentrismo. E continuare a spiegare le “ragioni” del geocentrismo fa un pessimo servizio a chi ascolta.

Post scriptum: i due fisici criticati da Battaglia per non essere scienziati dispongono delle seguenti credenziali bibliometriche Scopus (aggiornate ad agosto 2026):

Filippo Giorgi: 386 articoli, 47403 citazioni, h-index 111

Bruno Carli: 127 articoli, 1805 citazioni, h-index 23

A titolo di confronto, Franco Battaglia dispone di 27 articoli, quasi tutti precedenti al 1993 (33 anni fa) e nessuno inerente temi riconducibili al riscaldamento globale o i temi ambientali, 168 citazioni, h-index 8
